title: Contemplatives in action
hookLine: early Jesuits described themselves as contemplatives in action

lines: THE BELL CALLS THE CHOIR IN.
BUT WHAT IF YOU'RE ON A SHIP?
cards: You met the Society of Jesus back on day eight hundred forty-nine. Here's a puzzle its first members had to solve.
Catholic religious life had a beautiful rhythm: monks and nuns, and later friars, gathering in choir through the day to chant the psalms together. The bell rang, and everyone came in from the fields.
Ignatius and his companions wanted to be sent: to cities, to ports, to hospitals, to far countries, often alone. A bell in one chapel can't call a man who's on a ship.
So how does a person pray when the job is to keep moving?

teach.b: Their answer: contemplatives in action. The phrase is usually traced to Jerónimo Nadal, one of the early Jesuits, who traveled from house to house explaining the new order to its own members.
Describing Ignatius, he said, in Latin, that he was contemplative even in action. Not contemplative first and active second, in two shifts. Both at once.
So the new order made a choice that surprised people: the Jesuits did not gather in choir to chant the hours together the way monks and friars did.
Each one still prayed, went to Mass and kept the daily examen, but the shape of the day was built for movement. That was no judgment on the monasteries.
The Church keeps both, and the Carmelites, coming up soon on this path, will show the other shape. A different shape for a different job. What holds it together is yesterday's idea.
If God is at work in all things, then the classroom, the sickroom and the road aren't interruptions to prayer.

teach.h: THE ROAD IS WHERE PRAYER GOES.
teach.b: They're where prayer goes. Saint Paul packs it into three words in the Douay-Rheims: "Pray without ceasing."

Nobody can kneel without ceasing, but a person can carry a quiet awareness of God through a busy day, the way you carry a song in your head. Some worry this becomes an excuse: I'm too busy to pray; my work is my prayer.
The early Jesuits answered with the examen and the Exercises.

teach.h: STILL A STILL POINT TO RETURN TO.
teach.b: Action stays prayer only if there's still a still point to return to.

how: Jesuits and people formed in Ignatian spirituality try to pray in the midst of work and travel, anchored by Mass, personal prayer and the daily examen.

o: people who pray in the middle of work and travel
a busy life that counts its work as its only prayer
monks who pray in choir and work in the fields

games.q: contemplatives in action — tap the pairs.
p: chant the hours together in choir
a day built to be sent

s: the early Jesuits stopped praying so they could work
each still prayed, went to Mass and kept the examen. they just didn't chant the hours in choir.
the phrase is usually traced to Jerónimo Nadal, describing Ignatius
he said Ignatius was contemplative even in action.
choosing a traveling life was a judgment against monasteries
it was a different shape for a different job. the Church keeps both.

games.q: you're one of the first Jesuits. other orders gather in choir through the day to chant the psalms. your work is to be sent anywhere. what do you do?
o: keep the choir and travel less.
drop choir, and pray on the move with Mass and the examen.
drop prayer and just work hard.
games.why: the Jesuits did not keep choir. they built a day for movement, and kept a still point in Mass, personal prayer and the examen.

practice: Choose one simple task right where you are, folding a cloth, wiping a table, straightening your desk, and do it slowly, with full attention.
Let a short phrase ride along with each movement: if you pray, the name of Jesus, or Paul's pray without ceasing; if you don't, simply here, now.

wordCard.voice: Contemplatives in action. The early Jesuit ideal of praying in the middle of work and travel, not only apart from it, with the examen as the still point. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: contemplative in action, Nadal's description of Ignatius.

carryVoice: Your line: prayer in motion. The still point keeps the motion honest. Until tomorrow.
